passages.title: Ahaziah seeks an oracle and Elijah answers
passages.summary: King Ahaziah of Israel falls through a lattice and is badly hurt. He sends men to ask Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, if he will recover. Elijah meets them and asks whether Israel has no God. He says the king will die. Ahaziah sends a captain with fifty men to bring Elijah down. Fire from heaven burns them, and then a second fifty. A third captain kneels and begs for his men’s lives. Elijah goes with him, repeats the message, and the king dies.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How does the third captain’s request differ from the first two orders?

contextNote.title: A changed approach interrupts repeated violence
contextNote.text: The first two captains give orders in the king’s name (verses 9 and 11). Each treats the prophet as a man under royal command. The third captain in verse 13 comes on his knees. He asks for his life and the lives of his fifty. He has seen what a command produced. The angel then tells Elijah not to be afraid and to go (verse 15). Jesus later refuses a request to repeat this fire (Luke 9:54–55).

passages.title: Elijah departs and Elisha takes up the mantle
passages.summary: Elijah travels from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan. Three times he tells Elisha to stay, and Elisha refuses. Elijah strikes the river with his cloak, and they cross on dry ground. Elisha asks for a double share of his spirit. A chariot and horses of fire part them, and Elijah goes up in a whirlwind. Elisha takes up the fallen cloak and parts the Jordan again. He heals Jericho’s bad water with salt. Youths mock him near Bethel, and two bears maul forty-two of them.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The Institute manual connects the mantle with prophetic authority and distinguishes translation from resurrection. What does Elisha ask as he strikes the water (verse 14)?

contextNote.title: A repeated crossing makes succession visible
contextNote.text: Elijah parts the Jordan with his cloak in verse 8. In verse 14 Elisha does the same with the same cloak. His question asks for the God of Elijah, not for Elijah. The watching prophets draw the conclusion in verse 15. A “double portion” is the firstborn’s share in Deuteronomy 21:17. So Elisha asks to be the heir, not to be twice as great. A crossing of the Jordan also marked Joshua as Moses’s successor (Joshua 3:7).

passages.title: An alliance fights Moab
passages.summary: Jehoram of Israel goes to war when Moab stops paying tribute. Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom join him. After seven days the armies have no water. Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet, and they find Elisha. Elisha says he helps only for Jehoshaphat’s sake. He promises water without rain, and the valley fills by morning. Moab sees the water red as blood, attacks, and is routed. Moab’s king sacrifices his son on the wall, and Israel withdraws.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual proposes retreat after the heir’s death. It presents the reason as possible. What does Elisha tell Israel’s king to do in verse 13?

contextNote.title: An alliance does not remove differences among its members
contextNote.text: Three kings come to Elisha as allies. He does not treat them alike. In verse 13 he sends Israel’s king back to his parents’ prophets. Jehoram blames the LORD for the danger twice (verses 10 and 13). Elisha says he acts only out of regard for Jehoshaphat (verse 14). The ending in verse 27 is hard. The text reports “great wrath against Israel” and does not say whose.

passages.title: Oil, hospitality, a restored child, and food
passages.summary: A prophet’s widow tells Elisha that a creditor will take her two sons as slaves. She has only a jar of oil. He tells her to borrow empty jars and pour, and the oil fills them all. A wealthy woman of Shunem builds Elisha a room. He promises her a son, and the boy later dies in her lap. She rides to Elisha, and he prays and stretches out on the child. The boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Elisha also cures a poisoned stew and feeds a hundred men.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Elisha’s care and miracles with Christ’s ministry. What three things does Elisha tell the widow to do in verse 7?

contextNote.title: Household need gives prophetic work a practical setting
contextNote.text: The widow’s problem is a debt, and the law allowed creditors to take workers. Elisha starts with what she has in the house (verse 2). She must ask her neighbors for jars (verse 3). The oil stops when the jars run out (verse 6). So the amount matches what she gathered. Verse 7 turns the miracle into plain business: sell, pay, and live. Her sons stay free.

passages.title: Naaman accepts help and Gehazi pursues payment
passages.summary: Naaman commands the army of Syria, and he has a skin disease. A captive Israelite girl tells his wife about the prophet in Samaria. Naaman arrives with horses, chariots, and gifts. Elisha sends a messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is angry, but his servants persuade him. He washes and is healed, and he confesses Israel’s God. Elisha refuses any gift. His servant Gehazi runs after Naaman for silver and leaves with the disease.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me emphasizes humility and receiving help from people with less status. How do Naaman’s servants reason with him in verse 13?

contextNote.title: People below the commander help him receive healing
contextNote.text: Help reaches Naaman through people with no rank. A captive girl gives the first word (verses 2–3). The kings only exchange letters and panic (verses 5–7). Naaman expects a ceremony fit for a commander (verse 11). In verse 13 his servants reason with him gently. He would have done something hard, so why not something easy? Gehazi, the prophet’s own servant, then fails where foreign servants did well (verses 20–27).

passages.title: An axe floats, enemies receive food, and Samaria suffers
passages.summary: A borrowed axe head falls into the Jordan, and Elisha makes it float. He warns Israel’s king about Syrian ambushes again and again. Syria sends an army to seize him at Dothan. His servant panics until he sees horses and chariots of fire. The Syrians are struck blind, and Elisha leads them into Samaria. He tells the king to feed them and send them home. Later Syria besieges Samaria, and the famine is terrible. The king blames Elisha and swears to kill him.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses the servant’s opened eyes to teach trust in unseen divine help. What does Elisha tell the king to do with the captives (verse 22)?

contextNote.title: Capturing enemies need not end in killing them
contextNote.text: Israel’s king asks eagerly, twice, whether he may kill the prisoners (verse 21). Elisha’s answer in verse 22 has two parts. A king would not kill captives he took himself. These he did not even take. So he must set a meal before them. Verse 23 reports a great feast and an end to the raids. The peace is real but short, since verse 24 begins a siege.

passages.title: Four excluded men find an abandoned camp
passages.summary: Elisha says that by tomorrow flour will be cheap at Samaria’s gate. An officer scoffs, and Elisha says he will see it but not eat. Four men with skin disease sit outside the gate. They decide to surrender to the Syrians, since they will die anyway. They find the camp empty, because the LORD made the Syrians hear an army. They eat and hide silver, then decide to report it. The king suspects a trap and sends scouts. The people rush out for food, and the officer is trampled in the gate.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites trust in the fulfillment of God’s word. What do the four men decide in verse 9, and why?

contextNote.title: People kept outside become bearers of saving news
contextNote.text: Leviticus 13:46 kept people with this disease outside the camp. The four men sit at the gate of a starving city (verse 3). Their reasoning in verse 4 is plain arithmetic about death. At first they eat and hide treasure (verse 8). Verse 9 gives two motives for telling: it is not right, and punishment may come. Inside, the king doubts the news (verse 12). The city is fed through the men it kept out.

passages.title: The Shunammite returns and Hazael takes power
passages.summary: Elisha had warned the woman of Shunem about a seven-year famine. She lived among the Philistines and now returns. She appeals to the king for her house and land. At that moment Gehazi is telling the king about her son. The king restores her property and its income. Elisha goes to Damascus and weeps over what Hazael will do to Israel. Hazael smothers his sick king and takes the throne. In Judah, Jehoram marries Ahab’s daughter and follows Israel’s ways.

lds.text: What help does the Shunammite need after returning from famine?

contextNote.title: A household's lost land reaches the royal hearing
contextNote.text: In 4:13 this woman needed nothing from the king. She lived among her own people. Seven years away have cost her the house and fields (verse 3). Verse 5 notes the timing with “behold.” She arrives while her own story is being told. The text does not call it chance or design. The king gives back the land and all it produced since she left (verse 6).

passages.title: Jehu is anointed and kills the rulers
passages.summary: Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu, an army commander, as king. The message is to destroy Ahab’s house. Jehu’s fellow officers blow the trumpet and proclaim him. He drives furiously to Jezreel. King Joram rides out, and Jehu shoots him through the heart. The body is thrown onto Naboth’s field. Jehu’s men also kill Ahaziah king of Judah. Jezebel is thrown from a window, and dogs eat her body.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual distinguishes a predicted political outcome from approval of Jehu’s methods. Whose blood does verse 26 say the LORD has seen?

contextNote.title: A political killing receives meaning from an earlier theft
contextNote.text: Jehu remembers riding behind Ahab when the sentence was spoken (verse 25). In verse 26 he quotes it and names Naboth. This verse also mentions Naboth’s sons, which 1 Kings 21 did not. The body lands on the very plot that was stolen. So the text reads the killing as an answer to that theft. It does not thereby approve all that Jehu does next. Hosea 1:4 later speaks of punishment for the blood of Jezreel.

passages.title: Jehu destroys households and Baal’s sanctuary
passages.summary: Jehu writes to Samaria’s leaders, and they send him the heads of Ahab’s seventy sons. He kills all who remain of Ahab’s house in Jezreel. He also kills forty-two relatives of Judah’s king. He invites Jehonadab to see his zeal for the LORD. By a trick he gathers Baal’s worshipers into their temple and kills them. He destroys the temple and makes it a latrine. Yet he keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves. Hazael of Syria begins to take Israel’s land east of the Jordan.

lds.text: The older Church manual questions Jehu's motives. What does verse 31 say Jehu did not do?

contextNote.title: Removing one worship system does not complete reform
contextNote.text: Verse 28 says Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel. Verse 29 says he kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jeroboam set those up to secure his own kingdom (1 Kings 12:26–29). Jehu’s zeal stops where it would cost him the same security. He announced that zeal himself in verse 16. The praise in verse 30 covers only his work against Ahab’s house. Verse 31 measures him by the law and his whole heart.

passages.title: Joash is hidden and crowned
passages.summary: Athaliah, mother of the dead king of Judah, kills the royal children and rules. The king’s sister Jehosheba steals away the baby Joash. He is hidden in the temple for six years. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada brings in the guard captains. They surround the boy, crown him, and give him the covenant. Athaliah hears the noise and cries, “Treason!” She is put to death outside the temple. The people tear down Baal’s temple, and Joash takes the throne at seven.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual emphasizes the child’s protection and Jehoiada’s guidance. Where is the child kept for six years (verse 3)?

contextNote.title: A threatened royal line survives through concealed care
contextNote.text: Athaliah belongs to Ahab’s family (8:18 and 8:26). She is the only ruler of Judah in these books not from David’s line. Her killings leave one infant heir. Verse 2 credits an aunt and a nurse with saving him. Verse 3 covers six years in a single sentence. For six years David’s promised line rests on a hidden child (2 Samuel 7:16). No miracle is reported, only people who took a risk.

passages.title: Joash changes the temple repair system
passages.summary: Joash does right as long as the priest Jehoiada teaches him. He tells the priests to use offerings to repair the temple. After many years no repairs are done. Jehoiada sets a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar. The king’s scribe and the high priest count the silver. It is paid straight to carpenters, masons, and stonecutters. Later Hazael threatens Jerusalem, and Joash buys him off with temple treasure. His own servants kill him.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The older manual studies the collection system and Jehoiada’s support. Who was not asked to give an account in verse 15?

contextNote.title: Repair requires a system that reaches the workers
contextNote.text: The first plan let the priests collect money and manage repairs (verses 4–5). Verse 6 reports that nothing was fixed. The second plan separates the steps. Gifts go into a locked chest, and two officials count them (verses 9–10). The silver then goes directly to the workers (verses 11–12). Verse 15 says the foremen needed no audit because they were honest. Controls were placed at the point where the system had failed.

passages.title: Northern kings and Elisha’s death
passages.summary: Jehoahaz rules Israel, and Hazael of Syria crushes his army. He seeks the LORD, and Israel gets relief. His son Jehoash visits the dying Elisha and weeps over him. Elisha has him shoot an arrow east and calls it the LORD’s arrow of victory. He tells him to strike the ground with the other arrows. The king strikes three times and stops, and Elisha is angry. Elisha dies, and a dead man revives on touching his bones. Jehoash defeats Syria three times.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual connects Elisha’s arrows with victories over Syria. Why is Elisha angry in verse 19?

contextNote.title: An acted sign becomes a dispute about expectations
contextNote.text: The first arrow comes with its meaning stated: victory over Syria (verse 17). The king then knows what the arrows stand for. Told to strike the ground, he strikes three times and stops (verse 18). No number had been given. Elisha reads the stopping as a lack of resolve (verse 19). The text explains no further. Verse 25 counts exactly three victories.

passages.title: Amaziah loses a war and Jeroboam restores territory
passages.summary: Amaziah of Judah executes the servants who killed his father. He spares their children, as the law of Moses requires. He defeats Edom and then challenges Jehoash of Israel. Jehoash answers with a fable of a thistle and a cedar. Judah is beaten, Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and the temple gold is taken. Amaziah is later killed at Lachish. In Israel, Jeroboam the second rules forty-one years and does evil. Yet he restores Israel’s borders, as the prophet Jonah had said.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual studies Amaziah’s divided commitment and his failure to heed warning. What law does verse 6 quote?

contextNote.title: Restraint and ambition receive different judgments
contextNote.text: Verse 6 quotes Deuteronomy 24:16 nearly word for word. Each person dies for his own sin. Elsewhere in these books whole families die with the guilty (9:26; 10:7). Here the law limits a king’s revenge, and he keeps it. The same king then picks a fight he cannot win (verses 8–12). Verses 26–27 explain Jeroboam’s success. The LORD saw Israel’s suffering; the king’s merit is not the cause.

passages.title: Kings rise and fall as Assyria gains power
passages.summary: Azariah rules Judah fifty-two years and lives apart with a skin disease. In Israel, Zechariah rules six months and is murdered. Shallum lasts one month before Menahem kills him. Menahem pays the king of Assyria a thousand talents of silver to keep his throne. His son Pekahiah is killed by Pekah, an officer. Tiglath Pileser of Assyria takes Galilee and Gilead and deports the people. Hoshea kills Pekah and rules. In Judah, Jotham does right, but the high places remain.

lds.text: The older manual connects Uzziah’s account in Chronicles with respect for priesthood authority. Who pays the money in verse 20?

contextNote.title: A king's payment shifts an empire's demand onto households
contextNote.text: Four of Israel’s six kings in this chapter are murdered. Menahem keeps power another way. Verse 19 says he paid Assyria so its king would support his rule. Verse 20 shows who supplied the silver. Every wealthy man owed fifty shekels. The king’s safety is bought with his subjects’ money. In verse 29 Assyria returns anyway and carries people off.

passages.title: Ahaz seeks Assyrian help and changes the altar
passages.summary: Ahaz rules Judah and does not do right. He even burns his son as an offering. The kings of Syria and Israel attack Jerusalem. Ahaz sends temple silver to Tiglath Pileser and calls himself his servant and son. Assyria captures Damascus. Ahaz goes there, sees an altar, and sends its design to the priest Urijah. Urijah builds a copy, and the king offers on it. Ahaz moves the bronze altar and strips other temple furnishings because of Assyria’s king.

lds.text: How does Ahaz’s need for foreign help change temple worship?

contextNote.title: Foreign dependence changes the center of royal worship
contextNote.text: In verse 7 Ahaz calls himself the Assyrian king’s “servant” and “son.” Second Samuel 7:14 used “son” for the king’s bond with the LORD. Verse 10 shows the next step. The king sees a foreign altar and orders a copy for Jerusalem. The priest builds it without any recorded objection (verses 11 and 16). Verse 18 says other changes were made because of Assyria’s king. Isaiah 7 records the prophet’s advice to Ahaz in this same crisis.

passages.title: Samaria falls and the narrator explains exile
passages.summary: Hoshea of Israel stops paying Assyria and looks to Egypt. Assyria jails him and besieges Samaria for three years. The city falls, and Israel is carried away to Assyria. The writer explains that Israel served other gods and ignored every prophet. Judah also failed to keep the commandments. Assyria settles people from other lands in Samaria’s towns. Lions attack them, and a priest is sent back to teach about the LORD. They fear the LORD and also serve their own gods.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The older manual applies the fall to the need to heed prophetic warnings. Whom does Assyria settle in Samaria’s towns (verse 24)?

contextNote.title: Conquest changes both population and the account of belonging
contextNote.text: Assyria moves people in both directions. Israel goes out in verse 6, and five other peoples come in (verse 24). Each group brings its gods (verses 29–31). Verse 33 sums up the result: they feared the LORD and served their own gods. Verses 7–17 condemned Israel for that same mixture. The land has new people and the old problem. Verse 19 warns that Judah was no better.

passages.title: Hezekiah changes worship and faces Assyria
passages.summary: Hezekiah rules Judah and trusts the LORD more than any king before him. He removes the high places and breaks Moses’s bronze serpent, which people worshiped. He rebels against Assyria. Samaria falls in his sixth year. In his fourteenth year Sennacherib takes Judah’s walled towns. Hezekiah sends tribute and strips gold from the temple doors. Assyria still sends an army and a spokesman to Jerusalem. He shouts in Hebrew that no god has saved any land from Assyria.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Hezekiah’s trust during threats. What does Hezekiah say to the king of Assyria in verse 14?

contextNote.title: Two records describe royal power differently
contextNote.text: Verse 7 praises Hezekiah’s rebellion. Verse 13 shows its price: the loss of Judah’s fortified towns. In verse 14 he says, “I have offended,” and offers to pay. The gold comes from doors he himself had covered (verse 16). The payment does not stop the army (verse 17). Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. The two accounts share a setting but not a point of view.

passages.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
passages.summary: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah says not to fear the Assyrian’s words. The spokesman rejoins his king, who has left Lachish for Libnah. Sennacherib sends a letter mocking the LORD. Hezekiah spreads the letter out in the temple and prays. Isaiah answers that Assyria’s king will not enter the city or shoot an arrow there. That night the LORD’s angel strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me encourages prayer and trust when facing severe difficulties. What does Hezekiah do with the letter in verse 14?

contextNote.title: Lachish connects the speech with an actual campaign
contextNote.text: Verse 8 tracks the Assyrian king from Lachish to Libnah. That detail sets the threat to Jerusalem inside a wider war. The Lachish relief presents the conquest from Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings follows Judah’s crisis and its appeal for help. In chapter 18 Hezekiah answered with gold. In verse 14 he lays the letter before the LORD. His prayer asks that all kingdoms may know the LORD alone is God (verse 19).

passages.title: Hezekiah recovers and welcomes Babylon’s envoys
passages.summary: Hezekiah falls sick, and Isaiah tells him he will die. He turns to the wall, prays, and weeps. Before Isaiah leaves the palace, the LORD sends him back. Hezekiah will live fifteen more years, and the city will be saved. As a sign the shadow moves back ten steps. Envoys come from the king of Babylon with letters and a gift. Hezekiah shows them all his treasures and weapons. Isaiah says all of it, and some of his sons, will go to Babylon.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The older manual connects Hezekiah’s prayer with trust in divine care. What does verse 17 say will be left?

contextNote.title: Displayed wealth becomes an image of future loss
contextNote.text: Verse 13 stresses how much Hezekiah displayed. In verse 15 he says there is nothing he did not show. Verse 17 answers in the same terms: “Nothing will be left.” What he showed to Babylon will go to Babylon. Chapter 24:13 records the day it happened. Hezekiah’s reply in verse 19 accepts the word because his own days will be peaceful. The text reports that answer and leaves the reader to weigh it.

passages.title: Manasseh and Amon restore forbidden worship
passages.summary: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and rules fifty-five years. He rebuilds the high places his father Hezekiah destroyed. He sets up altars for Baal and for the stars inside the temple courts. He burns his son as an offering and uses sorcery. The prophets say Jerusalem will be wiped like a dish. Manasseh also sheds much innocent blood. His son Amon rules two years and is killed by his servants. The people make Amon’s son Josiah king.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Manasseh reverses many of Hezekiah's changes. How do a leader's choices affect other people?

contextNote.title: Worship criticism stands beside violence against people
contextNote.text: Most of the charges against Manasseh concern worship (verses 2–9). Verse 16 adds another kind “in addition”: innocent blood. It filled Jerusalem from one end to the other. The verse names no victims. Chapter 24:4 says this blood was what the LORD would not pardon. The longest reign in these books belongs to this king. Second Chronicles 33:12–13 records a repentance that Kings does not mention.

passages.title: The law scroll is found and Huldah responds
passages.summary: Josiah becomes king at eight and does what is right. In his eighteenth year he orders repairs to the temple. The high priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law there. The scribe Shaphan reads it to the king, and Josiah tears his clothes. He sends five officials to ask the LORD about it. They go to the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem. She says the book’s disaster will come on the city. Because Josiah humbled himself, he will not see it.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects scripture with changes of heart and commitment. To whom do the king’s officials go in verse 14?

contextNote.title: A discovered text requires interpretation before action
contextNote.text: The king’s most senior men carry the question. Verse 14 says they went to Huldah, a prophetess. She is identified by her husband’s post and her district of the city. Jeremiah was already active (Jeremiah 1:2), and the text gives no reason. She speaks in the LORD’s name without hesitation (verses 15–16). She calls the king “the man who sent you.” Her answer confirms the book and its warning.

passages.title: Josiah renews the covenant and removes shrines
passages.summary: Josiah reads the book of the covenant to all the people and renews the covenant. He removes Baal’s vessels and the Asherah pole from the temple. He defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba. He destroys the altar at Bethel, as a man of God had foretold. He orders a Passover such as had not been kept since the judges. No king before him turned to the LORD as he did. Still the LORD’s anger against Judah remains. Pharaoh Necoh kills Josiah at Megiddo, and Egypt chooses the next king.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Josiah’s promise to God. Which actions follow his reading of the law?

contextNote.title: Reform does not erase the account's accumulated judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 25 gives Josiah the highest praise in the book. Verse 26 begins with “Notwithstanding.” The reform is real, and it does not cancel the sentence. The list of things removed shows how deep the practices went. Much of it stood inside the temple itself (verses 4, 6–7, 11). Verses 15–18 fulfil the word spoken at Bethel in 1 Kings 13:2. Josiah dies in battle (verse 29), though 22:20 spoke of peace.

passages.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
passages.summary: Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon for three years and then rebels. Raiders attack Judah, as the prophets had said. His son Jehoiachin rules three months. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and the young king surrenders. Babylon takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Ten thousand people go into exile, including the king and his mother. Only the poorest remain in the land. Babylon makes Zedekiah king, and he too rebels.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual connects Zedekiah’s setting with Lehi in the Book of Mormon. This is an LDS cross-reference. Which groups does verse 14 say were taken away?

contextNote.title: Deportation removes the skills needed by a city
contextNote.text: Verse 14 lists who was taken: princes, soldiers, craftsmen, and smiths. These are the people who lead, defend, and make tools and weapons. Verse 14 also says who stayed: the poorest of the land. A city emptied this way cannot easily rebel again. Verse 13 fulfils Isaiah’s word to Hezekiah about the treasures (20:17). Verses 3–4 give the writer’s reason, the sins of Manasseh. Ezekiel 1:1–2 places that prophet among these exiles.

passages.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
passages.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for about two years, and famine grips the city. The wall is breached, and Zedekiah flees by night. He is caught, his sons are killed before him, and he is blinded. A month later the Babylonians burn the temple, the palace, and the houses. They break down the walls and carry off the bronze. Gedaliah is made governor and is soon murdered. The remaining people flee to Egypt. Years later Babylon’s new king frees Jehoiachin and feeds him at his table.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: What changes when Jehoiachin receives kindness at the end of the book?

contextNote.title: The ending preserves a narrow form of hope
contextNote.text: The book could have ended at verse 26 with the flight to Egypt. It adds four verses dated thirty-seven years into the exile. Verse 27 reports that a king of David’s line left prison. He receives a seat, new clothes, and daily food (verses 28–30). No return and no promise are stated. Second Samuel 7:15–16 had promised that David’s house would not be cut off. The ending shows that the line still lives, and says no more.

events.title: Ahaziah seeks an oracle and Elijah answers
events.summary: King Ahaziah of Israel falls through a lattice and is badly hurt. He sends men to ask Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, if he will recover. Elijah meets them and asks whether Israel has no God. He says the king will die. Ahaziah sends a captain with fifty men to bring Elijah down. Fire from heaven burns them, and then a second fifty. A third captain kneels and begs for his men’s lives. Elijah goes with him, repeats the message, and the king dies.
events.detail: The first two captains give orders in the king’s name (verses 9 and 11). Each treats the prophet as a man under royal command. The third captain in verse 13 comes on his knees. He asks for his life and the lives of his fifty. He has seen what a command produced. The angel then tells Elijah not to be afraid and to go (verse 15). Jesus later refuses a request to repeat this fire (Luke 9:54–55).

lds.text: How does the third captain’s request differ from the first two orders?

events.title: Elijah departs and Elisha takes up the mantle
events.summary: Elijah travels from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan. Three times he tells Elisha to stay, and Elisha refuses. Elijah strikes the river with his cloak, and they cross on dry ground. Elisha asks for a double share of his spirit. A chariot and horses of fire part them, and Elijah goes up in a whirlwind. Elisha takes up the fallen cloak and parts the Jordan again. He heals Jericho’s bad water with salt. Youths mock him near Bethel, and two bears maul forty-two of them.
events.detail: Elijah parts the Jordan with his cloak in verse 8. In verse 14 Elisha does the same with the same cloak. His question asks for the God of Elijah, not for Elijah. The watching prophets draw the conclusion in verse 15. A “double portion” is the firstborn’s share in Deuteronomy 21:17. So Elisha asks to be the heir, not to be twice as great. A crossing of the Jordan also marked Joshua as Moses’s successor (Joshua 3:7).

lds.text: The Institute manual connects the mantle with prophetic authority and distinguishes translation from resurrection. What does Elisha ask as he strikes the water (verse 14)?

events.title: An alliance fights Moab
events.summary: Jehoram of Israel goes to war when Moab stops paying tribute. Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom join him. After seven days the armies have no water. Jehoshaphat asks for a prophet, and they find Elisha. Elisha says he helps only for Jehoshaphat’s sake. He promises water without rain, and the valley fills by morning. Moab sees the water red as blood, attacks, and is routed. Moab’s king sacrifices his son on the wall, and Israel withdraws.
events.detail: Three kings come to Elisha as allies. He does not treat them alike. In verse 13 he sends Israel’s king back to his parents’ prophets. Jehoram blames the LORD for the danger twice (verses 10 and 13). Elisha says he acts only out of regard for Jehoshaphat (verse 14). The ending in verse 27 is hard. The text reports “great wrath against Israel” and does not say whose.
events.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: The older manual proposes retreat after the heir’s death. It presents the reason as possible. What does Elisha tell Israel’s king to do in verse 13?

events.title: Oil, hospitality, a restored child, and food
events.summary: A prophet’s widow tells Elisha that a creditor will take her two sons as slaves. She has only a jar of oil. He tells her to borrow empty jars and pour, and the oil fills them all. A wealthy woman of Shunem builds Elisha a room. He promises her a son, and the boy later dies in her lap. She rides to Elisha, and he prays and stretches out on the child. The boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Elisha also cures a poisoned stew and feeds a hundred men.
events.detail: The widow’s problem is a debt, and the law allowed creditors to take workers. Elisha starts with what she has in the house (verse 2). She must ask her neighbors for jars (verse 3). The oil stops when the jars run out (verse 6). So the amount matches what she gathered. Verse 7 turns the miracle into plain business: sell, pay, and live. Her sons stay free.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects Elisha’s care and miracles with Christ’s ministry. What three things does Elisha tell the widow to do in verse 7?

events.title: Naaman accepts help and Gehazi pursues payment
events.summary: Naaman commands the army of Syria, and he has a skin disease. A captive Israelite girl tells his wife about the prophet in Samaria. Naaman arrives with horses, chariots, and gifts. Elisha sends a messenger: wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is angry, but his servants persuade him. He washes and is healed, and he confesses Israel’s God. Elisha refuses any gift. His servant Gehazi runs after Naaman for silver and leaves with the disease.
events.detail: Help reaches Naaman through people with no rank. A captive girl gives the first word (verses 2–3). The kings only exchange letters and panic (verses 5–7). Naaman expects a ceremony fit for a commander (verse 11). In verse 13 his servants reason with him gently. He would have done something hard, so why not something easy? Gehazi, the prophet’s own servant, then fails where foreign servants did well (verses 20–27).

lds.text: Come, Follow Me emphasizes humility and receiving help from people with less status. How do Naaman’s servants reason with him in verse 13?

events.title: An axe floats, enemies receive food, and Samaria suffers
events.summary: A borrowed axe head falls into the Jordan, and Elisha makes it float. He warns Israel’s king about Syrian ambushes again and again. Syria sends an army to seize him at Dothan. His servant panics until he sees horses and chariots of fire. The Syrians are struck blind, and Elisha leads them into Samaria. He tells the king to feed them and send them home. Later Syria besieges Samaria, and the famine is terrible. The king blames Elisha and swears to kill him.
events.detail: Israel’s king asks eagerly, twice, whether he may kill the prisoners (verse 21). Elisha’s answer in verse 22 has two parts. A king would not kill captives he took himself. These he did not even take. So he must set a meal before them. Verse 23 reports a great feast and an end to the raids. The peace is real but short, since verse 24 begins a siege.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places 2 Kings names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses the servant’s opened eyes to teach trust in unseen divine help. What does Elisha tell the king to do with the captives (verse 22)?

events.title: Four excluded men find an abandoned camp
events.summary: Elisha says that by tomorrow flour will be cheap at Samaria’s gate. An officer scoffs, and Elisha says he will see it but not eat. Four men with skin disease sit outside the gate. They decide to surrender to the Syrians, since they will die anyway. They find the camp empty, because the LORD made the Syrians hear an army. They eat and hide silver, then decide to report it. The king suspects a trap and sends scouts. The people rush out for food, and the officer is trampled in the gate.
events.detail: Leviticus 13:46 kept people with this disease outside the camp. The four men sit at the gate of a starving city (verse 3). Their reasoning in verse 4 is plain arithmetic about death. At first they eat and hide treasure (verse 8). Verse 9 gives two motives for telling: it is not right, and punishment may come. Inside, the king doubts the news (verse 12). The city is fed through the men it kept out.
events.uncertainty: Points show the towns and regions the chapter names. Some sites are proposed or disputed, so positions are approximate.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites trust in the fulfillment of God’s word. What do the four men decide in verse 9, and why?

events.title: The Shunammite returns and Hazael takes power
events.summary: Elisha had warned the woman of Shunem about a seven-year famine. She lived among the Philistines and now returns. She appeals to the king for her house and land. At that moment Gehazi is telling the king about her son. The king restores her property and its income. Elisha goes to Damascus and weeps over what Hazael will do to Israel. Hazael smothers his sick king and takes the throne. In Judah, Jehoram marries Ahab’s daughter and follows Israel’s ways.
events.detail: In 4:13 this woman needed nothing from the king. She lived among her own people. Seven years away have cost her the house and fields (verse 3). Verse 5 notes the timing with “behold.” She arrives while her own story is being told. The text does not call it chance or design. The king gives back the land and all it produced since she left (verse 6).

events.title: Jehu is anointed and kills the rulers
events.summary: Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu, an army commander, as king. The message is to destroy Ahab’s house. Jehu’s fellow officers blow the trumpet and proclaim him. He drives furiously to Jezreel. King Joram rides out, and Jehu shoots him through the heart. The body is thrown onto Naboth’s field. Jehu’s men also kill Ahaziah king of Judah. Jezebel is thrown from a window, and dogs eat her body.
events.detail: Jehu remembers riding behind Ahab when the sentence was spoken (verse 25). In verse 26 he quotes it and names Naboth. This verse also mentions Naboth’s sons, which 1 Kings 21 did not. The body lands on the very plot that was stolen. So the text reads the killing as an answer to that theft. It does not thereby approve all that Jehu does next. Hosea 1:4 later speaks of punishment for the blood of Jezreel.

events.title: Jehu destroys households and Baal’s sanctuary
events.summary: Jehu writes to Samaria’s leaders, and they send him the heads of Ahab’s seventy sons. He kills all who remain of Ahab’s house in Jezreel. He also kills forty-two relatives of Judah’s king. He invites Jehonadab to see his zeal for the LORD. By a trick he gathers Baal’s worshipers into their temple and kills them. He destroys the temple and makes it a latrine. Yet he keeps Jeroboam’s golden calves. Hazael of Syria begins to take Israel’s land east of the Jordan.
events.detail: Verse 28 says Jehu destroyed Baal out of Israel. Verse 29 says he kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. Jeroboam set those up to secure his own kingdom (1 Kings 12:26–29). Jehu’s zeal stops where it would cost him the same security. He announced that zeal himself in verse 16. The praise in verse 30 covers only his work against Ahab’s house. Verse 31 measures him by the law and his whole heart.

events.title: Joash is hidden and crowned
events.summary: Athaliah, mother of the dead king of Judah, kills the royal children and rules. The king’s sister Jehosheba steals away the baby Joash. He is hidden in the temple for six years. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada brings in the guard captains. They surround the boy, crown him, and give him the covenant. Athaliah hears the noise and cries, “Treason!” She is put to death outside the temple. The people tear down Baal’s temple, and Joash takes the throne at seven.
events.detail: Athaliah belongs to Ahab’s family (8:18 and 8:26). She is the only ruler of Judah in these books not from David’s line. Her killings leave one infant heir. Verse 2 credits an aunt and a nurse with saving him. Verse 3 covers six years in a single sentence. For six years David’s promised line rests on a hidden child (2 Samuel 7:16). No miracle is reported, only people who took a risk.

events.title: Joash changes the temple repair system
events.summary: Joash does right as long as the priest Jehoiada teaches him. He tells the priests to use offerings to repair the temple. After many years no repairs are done. Jehoiada sets a chest with a hole in its lid beside the altar. The king’s scribe and the high priest count the silver. It is paid straight to carpenters, masons, and stonecutters. Later Hazael threatens Jerusalem, and Joash buys him off with temple treasure. His own servants kill him.
events.detail: The first plan let the priests collect money and manage repairs (verses 4–5). Verse 6 reports that nothing was fixed. The second plan separates the steps. Gifts go into a locked chest, and two officials count them (verses 9–10). The silver then goes directly to the workers (verses 11–12). Verse 15 says the foremen needed no audit because they were honest. Controls were placed at the point where the system had failed.

events.title: Northern kings and Elisha’s death
events.summary: Jehoahaz rules Israel, and Hazael of Syria crushes his army. He seeks the LORD, and Israel gets relief. His son Jehoash visits the dying Elisha and weeps over him. Elisha has him shoot an arrow east and calls it the LORD’s arrow of victory. He tells him to strike the ground with the other arrows. The king strikes three times and stops, and Elisha is angry. Elisha dies, and a dead man revives on touching his bones. Jehoash defeats Syria three times.
events.detail: The first arrow comes with its meaning stated: victory over Syria (verse 17). The king then knows what the arrows stand for. Told to strike the ground, he strikes three times and stops (verse 18). No number had been given. Elisha reads the stopping as a lack of resolve (verse 19). The text explains no further. Verse 25 counts exactly three victories.

events.title: Amaziah loses a war and Jeroboam restores territory
events.summary: Amaziah of Judah executes the servants who killed his father. He spares their children, as the law of Moses requires. He defeats Edom and then challenges Jehoash of Israel. Jehoash answers with a fable of a thistle and a cedar. Judah is beaten, Jerusalem’s wall is broken, and the temple gold is taken. Amaziah is later killed at Lachish. In Israel, Jeroboam the second rules forty-one years and does evil. Yet he restores Israel’s borders, as the prophet Jonah had said.
events.detail: Verse 6 quotes Deuteronomy 24:16 nearly word for word. Each person dies for his own sin. Elsewhere in these books whole families die with the guilty (9:26; 10:7). Here the law limits a king’s revenge, and he keeps it. The same king then picks a fight he cannot win (verses 8–12). Verses 26–27 explain Jeroboam’s success. The LORD saw Israel’s suffering; the king’s merit is not the cause.

events.title: Kings rise and fall as Assyria gains power
events.summary: Azariah rules Judah fifty-two years and lives apart with a skin disease. In Israel, Zechariah rules six months and is murdered. Shallum lasts one month before Menahem kills him. Menahem pays the king of Assyria a thousand talents of silver to keep his throne. His son Pekahiah is killed by Pekah, an officer. Tiglath Pileser of Assyria takes Galilee and Gilead and deports the people. Hoshea kills Pekah and rules. In Judah, Jotham does right, but the high places remain.
events.detail: Four of Israel’s six kings in this chapter are murdered. Menahem keeps power another way. Verse 19 says he paid Assyria so its king would support his rule. Verse 20 shows who supplied the silver. Every wealthy man owed fifty shekels. The king’s safety is bought with his subjects’ money. In verse 29 Assyria returns anyway and carries people off.

events.title: Ahaz seeks Assyrian help and changes the altar
events.summary: Ahaz rules Judah and does not do right. He even burns his son as an offering. The kings of Syria and Israel attack Jerusalem. Ahaz sends temple silver to Tiglath Pileser and calls himself his servant and son. Assyria captures Damascus. Ahaz goes there, sees an altar, and sends its design to the priest Urijah. Urijah builds a copy, and the king offers on it. Ahaz moves the bronze altar and strips other temple furnishings because of Assyria’s king.
events.detail: In verse 7 Ahaz calls himself the Assyrian king’s “servant” and “son.” Second Samuel 7:14 used “son” for the king’s bond with the LORD. Verse 10 shows the next step. The king sees a foreign altar and orders a copy for Jerusalem. The priest builds it without any recorded objection (verses 11 and 16). Verse 18 says other changes were made because of Assyria’s king. Isaiah 7 records the prophet’s advice to Ahaz in this same crisis.

events.title: Samaria falls and the narrator explains exile
events.summary: Hoshea of Israel stops paying Assyria and looks to Egypt. Assyria jails him and besieges Samaria for three years. The city falls, and Israel is carried away to Assyria. The writer explains that Israel served other gods and ignored every prophet. Judah also failed to keep the commandments. Assyria settles people from other lands in Samaria’s towns. Lions attack them, and a priest is sent back to teach about the LORD. They fear the LORD and also serve their own gods.
events.detail: Assyria moves people in both directions. Israel goes out in verse 6, and five other peoples come in (verse 24). Each group brings its gods (verses 29–31). Verse 33 sums up the result: they feared the LORD and served their own gods. Verses 7–17 condemned Israel for that same mixture. The land has new people and the old problem. Verse 19 warns that Judah was no better.

events.title: Hezekiah changes worship and faces Assyria
events.summary: Hezekiah rules Judah and trusts the LORD more than any king before him. He removes the high places and breaks Moses’s bronze serpent, which people worshiped. He rebels against Assyria. Samaria falls in his sixth year. In his fourteenth year Sennacherib takes Judah’s walled towns. Hezekiah sends tribute and strips gold from the temple doors. Assyria still sends an army and a spokesman to Jerusalem. He shouts in Hebrew that no god has saved any land from Assyria.
events.detail: Verse 7 praises Hezekiah’s rebellion. Verse 13 shows its price: the loss of Judah’s fortified towns. In verse 14 he says, “I have offended,” and offers to pay. The gold comes from doors he himself had covered (verse 16). The payment does not stop the army (verse 17). Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. The two accounts share a setting but not a point of view.

events.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
events.summary: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah says not to fear the Assyrian’s words. The spokesman rejoins his king, who has left Lachish for Libnah. Sennacherib sends a letter mocking the LORD. Hezekiah spreads the letter out in the temple and prays. Isaiah answers that Assyria’s king will not enter the city or shoot an arrow there. That night the LORD’s angel strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.
events.detail: Verse 8 tracks the Assyrian king from Lachish to Libnah. That detail sets the threat to Jerusalem inside a wider war. The Lachish relief presents the conquest from Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings follows Judah’s crisis and its appeal for help. In chapter 18 Hezekiah answered with gold. In verse 14 he lays the letter before the LORD. His prayer asks that all kingdoms may know the LORD alone is God (verse 19).

events.title: Hezekiah recovers and welcomes Babylon’s envoys
events.summary: Hezekiah falls sick, and Isaiah tells him he will die. He turns to the wall, prays, and weeps. Before Isaiah leaves the palace, the LORD sends him back. Hezekiah will live fifteen more years, and the city will be saved. As a sign the shadow moves back ten steps. Envoys come from the king of Babylon with letters and a gift. Hezekiah shows them all his treasures and weapons. Isaiah says all of it, and some of his sons, will go to Babylon.
events.detail: Verse 13 stresses how much Hezekiah displayed. In verse 15 he says there is nothing he did not show. Verse 17 answers in the same terms: “Nothing will be left.” What he showed to Babylon will go to Babylon. Chapter 24:13 records the day it happened. Hezekiah’s reply in verse 19 accepts the word because his own days will be peaceful. The text reports that answer and leaves the reader to weigh it.

events.title: Manasseh and Amon restore forbidden worship
events.summary: Manasseh becomes king at twelve and rules fifty-five years. He rebuilds the high places his father Hezekiah destroyed. He sets up altars for Baal and for the stars inside the temple courts. He burns his son as an offering and uses sorcery. The prophets say Jerusalem will be wiped like a dish. Manasseh also sheds much innocent blood. His son Amon rules two years and is killed by his servants. The people make Amon’s son Josiah king.
events.detail: Most of the charges against Manasseh concern worship (verses 2–9). Verse 16 adds another kind “in addition”: innocent blood. It filled Jerusalem from one end to the other. The verse names no victims. Chapter 24:4 says this blood was what the LORD would not pardon. The longest reign in these books belongs to this king. Second Chronicles 33:12–13 records a repentance that Kings does not mention.

events.title: The law scroll is found and Huldah responds
events.summary: Josiah becomes king at eight and does what is right. In his eighteenth year he orders repairs to the temple. The high priest Hilkiah finds the book of the law there. The scribe Shaphan reads it to the king, and Josiah tears his clothes. He sends five officials to ask the LORD about it. They go to the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem. She says the book’s disaster will come on the city. Because Josiah humbled himself, he will not see it.
events.detail: The king’s most senior men carry the question. Verse 14 says they went to Huldah, a prophetess. She is identified by her husband’s post and her district of the city. Jeremiah was already active (Jeremiah 1:2), and the text gives no reason. She speaks in the LORD’s name without hesitation (verses 15–16). She calls the king “the man who sent you.” Her answer confirms the book and its warning.

events.title: Josiah renews the covenant and removes shrines
events.summary: Josiah reads the book of the covenant to all the people and renews the covenant. He removes Baal’s vessels and the Asherah pole from the temple. He defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba. He destroys the altar at Bethel, as a man of God had foretold. He orders a Passover such as had not been kept since the judges. No king before him turned to the LORD as he did. Still the LORD’s anger against Judah remains. Pharaoh Necoh kills Josiah at Megiddo, and Egypt chooses the next king.
events.detail: Verse 25 gives Josiah the highest praise in the book. Verse 26 begins with “Notwithstanding.” The reform is real, and it does not cancel the sentence. The list of things removed shows how deep the practices went. Much of it stood inside the temple itself (verses 4, 6–7, 11). Verses 15–18 fulfil the word spoken at Bethel in 1 Kings 13:2. Josiah dies in battle (verse 29), though 22:20 spoke of peace.

events.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
events.summary: Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon for three years and then rebels. Raiders attack Judah, as the prophets had said. His son Jehoiachin rules three months. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and the young king surrenders. Babylon takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Ten thousand people go into exile, including the king and his mother. Only the poorest remain in the land. Babylon makes Zedekiah king, and he too rebels.
events.detail: Verse 14 lists who was taken: princes, soldiers, craftsmen, and smiths. These are the people who lead, defend, and make tools and weapons. Verse 14 also says who stayed: the poorest of the land. A city emptied this way cannot easily rebel again. Verse 13 fulfils Isaiah’s word to Hezekiah about the treasures (20:17). Verses 3–4 give the writer’s reason, the sins of Manasseh. Ezekiel 1:1–2 places that prophet among these exiles.

events.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
events.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for about two years, and famine grips the city. The wall is breached, and Zedekiah flees by night. He is caught, his sons are killed before him, and he is blinded. A month later the Babylonians burn the temple, the palace, and the houses. They break down the walls and carry off the bronze. Gedaliah is made governor and is soon murdered. The remaining people flee to Egypt. Years later Babylon’s new king frees Jehoiachin and feeds him at his table.
events.detail: The book could have ended at verse 26 with the flight to Egypt. It adds four verses dated thirty-seven years into the exile. Verse 27 reports that a king of David’s line left prison. He receives a seat, new clothes, and daily food (verses 28–30). No return and no promise are stated. Second Samuel 7:15–16 had promised that David’s house would not be cut off. The ending shows that the line still lives, and says no more.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Kingdom of Israel · approximate

guides.title: 2 Kings: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Two records describe royal power differently
steps.text: Verse 7 praises Hezekiah’s rebellion. Verse 13 shows its price: the loss of Judah’s fortified towns. In verse 14 he says, “I have offended,” and offers to pay. The gold comes from doors he himself had covered (verse 16). The payment does not stop the army (verse 17). Assyrian royal records also present this campaign from the conqueror’s side. The two accounts share a setting but not a point of view.

steps.title: Lachish connects the speech with an actual campaign
steps.text: Verse 8 tracks the Assyrian king from Lachish to Libnah. That detail sets the threat to Jerusalem inside a wider war. The Lachish relief presents the conquest from Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings follows Judah’s crisis and its appeal for help. In chapter 18 Hezekiah answered with gold. In verse 14 he lays the letter before the LORD. His prayer asks that all kingdoms may know the LORD alone is God (verse 19).

steps.title: The ending preserves a narrow form of hope
steps.text: The book could have ended at verse 26 with the flight to Egypt. It adds four verses dated thirty-seven years into the exile. Verse 27 reports that a king of David’s line left prison. He receives a seat, new clothes, and daily food (verses 28–30). No return and no promise are stated. Second Samuel 7:15–16 had promised that David’s house would not be cut off. The ending shows that the line still lives, and says no more.

textRoutes.title: Elijah departs and Elisha takes up the mantle
textRoutes.summary: Elijah travels from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan. Three times he tells Elisha to stay, and Elisha refuses. textRoutes.detail: Elijah parts the Jordan with his cloak in verse 8. In verse 14 Elisha does the same with the same cloak. His question asks for the God of Elijah, not for Elijah. The watching prophets draw the conclusion in verse 15. A “double portion” is the firstborn’s share in Deuteronomy 21:17. So Elisha asks to be the heir, not to be twice as great. A crossing of the Jordan also marked Joshua as Moses’s successor (Joshua 3:7).

textRoutes.detail: In verse 7 Ahaz calls himself the Assyrian king’s “servant” and “son.” Second Samuel 7:14 used “son” for the king’s bond with the LORD. Verse 10 shows the next step. The king sees a foreign altar and orders a copy for Jerusalem. The priest builds it without any recorded objection (verses 11 and 16). Verse 18 says other changes were made because of Assyria’s king. Isaiah 7 records the prophet’s advice to Ahaz in this same crisis.

textRoutes.title: Hezekiah prays and Isaiah answers
textRoutes.summary: Hezekiah tears his clothes and sends to the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah says not to fear the Assyrian’s words. The spokesman rejoins his king, who has left Lachish for Libnah. Sennacherib sends a letter mocking the LORD. Hezekiah spreads the letter out in the temple and prays. Isaiah answers that Assyria’s king will not enter the city or shoot an arrow there. That night the LORD’s angel strikes the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, where his sons kill him.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 8 tracks the Assyrian king from Lachish to Libnah. That detail sets the threat to Jerusalem inside a wider war. The Lachish relief presents the conquest from Assyria’s royal viewpoint. Kings follows Judah’s crisis and its appeal for help. In chapter 18 Hezekiah answered with gold. In verse 14 he lays the letter before the LORD. His prayer asks that all kingdoms may know the LORD alone is God (verse 19).

textRoutes.title: Babylon takes treasure and deports Jehoiachin
textRoutes.summary: Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon for three years and then rebels. Raiders attack Judah, as the prophets had said. His son Jehoiachin rules three months. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and the young king surrenders. Babylon takes the treasures of the temple and palace. Ten thousand people go into exile, including the king and his mother. Only the poorest remain in the land. Babylon makes Zedekiah king, and he too rebels.
textRoutes.detail: Verse 14 lists who was taken: princes, soldiers, craftsmen, and smiths. These are the people who lead, defend, and make tools and weapons. Verse 14 also says who stayed: the poorest of the land. A city emptied this way cannot easily rebel again. Verse 13 fulfils Isaiah’s word to Hezekiah about the treasures (20:17). Verses 3–4 give the writer’s reason, the sins of Manasseh. Ezekiel 1:1–2 places that prophet among these exiles.

textRoutes.title: Jerusalem is destroyed and a prisoner receives favor
textRoutes.summary: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for about two years, and famine grips the city. The wall is breached, and Zedekiah flees by night. He is caught, his sons are killed before him, and he is blinded. A month later the Babylonians burn the temple, the palace, and the houses. They break down the walls and carry off the bronze. Gedaliah is made governor and is soon murdered. The remaining people flee to Egypt. Years later Babylon’s new king frees Jehoiachin and feeds him at his table.
textRoutes.detail: The book could have ended at verse 26 with the flight to Egypt. It adds four verses dated thirty-seven years into the exile. Verse 27 reports that a king of David’s line left prison. He receives a seat, new clothes, and daily food (verses 28–30). No return and no promise are stated. Second Samuel 7:15–16 had promised that David’s house would not be cut off. The ending shows that the line still lives, and says no more.
